blocks.html: Logic is the study of good reasoning, and reasoning is built from statements. Before we can weigh an argument, we need to know which sentences can be its parts. This is the first rung of the Logic Ladder, so we start from scratch.
A statement is a sentence that is either true or false. Questions, commands, requests and exclamations are not statements, because they do not claim that anything is so.

Reasons work by passing truth along: if these claims are true, that claim must be (or probably is) true too. Only a sentence that can be true or false can take part. "Please pass the salt" can be polite or rude, but never true or false, so it cannot be a reason for anything.

A statement does not have to be true. "Seven is an even number" is false, and it is still a statement. It also does not have to be a fact everyone agrees on. "Soccer is more fun than chess" is an opinion, but it claims something that people can agree or disagree with, so it counts.

blocks.name: lg-sort

opts.task: Sort each sentence. Then press Check.

cards.text: Owls hunt mostly at night.
cards.why: A true claim about owls.

cards.text: Please close the window.
cards.why: A request is neither true nor false.

cards.text: There are nine planets in our solar system.
cards.why: It is false (there are eight), but a false claim is still a statement.

cards.text: Is the library open on Sunday?
cards.why: A question asks; it does not claim.

cards.text: Pizza is the best food.
cards.why: An opinion still makes a claim, so it is a statement.

cards.text: What a sunset!
cards.why: An exclamation shows a feeling but claims nothing.

blocks.cap: Tap a card, then a group. A false claim and an opinion both count as statements.

blocks.title: Statement or not?
blocks.q: Which of these are statements? (a) "Spiders have six legs." (b) "Bring your coat." (c) "It will rain tomorrow."
steps: (a) claims something about spiders. It is false (spiders have eight legs), but it is still a statement.
(b) tells someone to act. It cannot be true or false, so it is not a statement.
(c) is a prediction. We do not know yet whether it is true, but it will turn out true or false, so it is a statement.

blocks.html: Thinking a statement must be true, or that an opinion cannot be a statement. "Pizza is the best food" is a statement: it is simply one that people disagree about. Quick check: could someone sensibly reply "That's true" or "That's false"? If so, it is a statement.
A question can sometimes hint at a claim ("Isn't it cold in here?" hints "It is cold"). In this course we take sentences at face value: a question is not a statement.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.2 Logical Statements
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (statements, arguments, premises and conclusions)

blocks.html: You know what a statement is: a sentence that is true or false. An argument is a group of statements where some are offered as reasons for another. In logic, an argument is not a quarrel; it is a case made with reasons.
An argument has a conclusion (the claim to be accepted) and at least one premise (a reason offered for it). A passage with no reason offered for a claim is not an argument.

The point of an argument is to give someone a reason to believe something they might doubt. If a passage only describes, reports, warns, or states a view without support, there is nothing for a listener to weigh: no "because", stated or implied.

head: Passage
Argument?
rows: "The pool closes at six, and it's already half past five. So we won't have time to swim."
Yes: two reasons support a conclusion.
"The pool opened in 1985. It has a diving board."
"Swimming is the best sport. Nothing will change my mind."
No: a bare opinion, said twice.
blocks.cap: Arguments and some common non-arguments.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: You should bring a jacket, since the forecast says it will be cold.
Last Tuesday the club met and planned the spring fair.
cards.why: A report of events: no claim is supported.

cards.text: The puppy must be hungry, because it hasn't eaten since morning.
I love history. It is my favorite subject by far.
cards.why: Saying an opinion twice is not giving a reason for it.

cards.text: If the bus is late, we will miss the opening.
cards.why: One if-then sentence is a single claim.

blocks.cap: Look for a claim and a reason offered for it.

blocks.title: Find the reason
blocks.q: "Our class should plant tomatoes. They grow well in full sun, and our garden gets sun all day." Is this an argument?
steps: Look for the claim the speaker wants us to accept: "Our class should plant tomatoes."
Look for reasons: tomatoes grow well in full sun; the garden gets sun all day.
Reasons are offered for a claim, so this is an argument.

blocks.html: Calling a strong opinion an argument. "This movie is terrible, the worst ever!" is forceful, but force is not a reason. Ask: what reason is offered? If you cannot point to one, it is an assertion, not an argument.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.3 Arguments
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (recognizing arguments)

blocks.html: An argument offers reasons for a claim. Explanations look almost the same, and both often use "because". The difference is in their job.
An argument tries to show that a claim is true. An explanation tells why or how something we already accept is true.

Ask whether the main claim is in doubt. "The game was cancelled because the field flooded" is said after everyone knows the game was cancelled; the speaker is giving its cause. "The game will probably be cancelled, because the field is flooding" tries to convince you of something you do not know yet.

head: Argument
Explanation
blocks.cap: Two jobs for "because".

blocks.title: Which job?
blocks.q: "The ice on the pond melted because the weather turned warm this week."
steps: Is anyone in doubt that the ice melted? No: it is plain to see.
The "because" part gives the cause: warm weather.
So the passage explains why the ice melted.

blocks.title: Same word, other job
blocks.q: "The cat is probably sick, because it hasn't eaten in two days and it is hiding."
steps: Is it known that the cat is sick? No: that is the question.
The "because" part gives evidence: not eating and hiding.
So the passage is trying to show the cat is sick.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: Leaves change color in fall because the green pigment breaks down.
cards.why: That leaves change color is known; this tells how.

cards.text: Ben must have left already, because his coat is gone from the hook.
cards.why: Whether Ben left is in doubt; the coat is evidence.

cards.text: The bread rose because the yeast made bubbles of gas.
We should plant next week, because the last frost will be over by then.

blocks.cap: Ask of each: is the main claim in doubt, or already accepted?

blocks.html: Treating every "because" as an argument. The word appears in both. Check by asking: would the listener have doubted the main claim before hearing the reason? If not, it is an explanation.

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (arguments and explanations)
OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.3 Arguments

blocks.html: Every argument has two kinds of parts. To read one well, you first sort its sentences into the claim being argued for and the reasons for it.
The conclusion is what the speaker wants you to believe. The premises are the reasons offered for it. Find the conclusion first; then the premises are the sentences that support it.

A sentence is a premise or a conclusion because of the job it does in this argument, not because of where it sits. The same claim, "We need to leave by seven," can be a conclusion in one argument and a premise in another ("We need to leave by seven, so set an alarm").

blocks.name: lg-argmap

sentences.text: We need to leave by seven.
The concert starts at eight.
And the drive takes almost an hour.

blocks.cap: Label each sentence, then press Check. Here the conclusion comes first.

blocks.title: Conclusion in the middle
blocks.q: "The lights are on at Ava's house. Ava must be home. Besides, her bike is in the driveway."
steps: Ask: what does the speaker want me to believe? That Ava is home.
The lights and the bike are offered as reasons for that.
So the conclusion is the middle sentence; the other two are premises.
blocks.a: Conclusion: "Ava must be home." Premises: the lights are on; the bike is in the driveway.

blocks.title: Ask "why should I believe that?"
blocks.q: "The library's history books are all checked out. The report is due Friday. So Kai had better start looking online."
steps: Try each sentence as the conclusion and ask "Why should I believe that?"
"Why should Kai look online?" Because the books are out and the report is due soon. The other sentences answer it.
Nothing answers "Why are the books checked out?" in the passage, so that sentence is a premise.
blocks.a: Conclusion: "Kai had better start looking online."

blocks.html: Assuming the first sentence is a premise and the last one is the conclusion. Writers often lead with the conclusion. Test each candidate: the conclusion is the one the others are reasons for.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.3 Arguments
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (arguments, premises and conclusions)

blocks.html: Finding premises and conclusions is easier when the writer leaves signposts. These signposts are called indicator words.
Conclusion indicators come before a conclusion: therefore, so, thus, hence, consequently, it follows that. Premise indicators come before a premise: because, since, for, given that, after all.

Indicator words show the direction of support. "The road is icy, so drive slowly" and "Drive slowly, because the road is icy" say the same thing in two orders; the word tells you which claim supports which.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

opts.passage: We should leave for the game early, since the road by the stadium is closed. The detour adds twenty minutes, so the earlier the better.

nodes.text: The road by the stadium is closed.
The detour adds twenty minutes.
We should leave for the game early.

blocks.cap: Blue marks a conclusion indicator; gold marks a premise indicator.

blocks.title: Follow the signpost
blocks.q: "Since the store is closed, we will buy bread tomorrow."
steps: "Since" is a premise indicator, so "the store is closed" is a premise.
The other claim, "we will buy bread tomorrow", is the conclusion.

blocks.html: Trusting the word without reading the sentence. Indicator words have other jobs: "We have been friends since second grade" is about time, "I was so tired" means very, and "a gift for Mom" says who it is for. Quick check: swap in "because" or "therefore". If the sentence stops making sense, the word is not an indicator there.

blocks.title: Not an indicator
blocks.q: "I was so hungry after practice." Is "so" a conclusion indicator here?
steps: Swap in "therefore": "I was therefore hungry after practice." The meaning changes.
Here "so" means "very". No conclusion is being drawn.
blocks.a: No, it is not an indicator here.

blocks.html: Many arguments have no indicator words at all. Then go back to the main test: which claim do the others support?

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (premise and conclusion indicators)
OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.3 Arguments

blocks.html: Once you can find premises and conclusions, you can write an argument out cleanly. Logicians call this standard form.
Standard form: list the premises, numbered, one claim per line, then the conclusion last, marked with "So". Leave out filler, repeats and side remarks, and keep each claim's meaning exactly.

Real arguments come mixed with greetings, stories and asides. Laying out only the reasons and the claim they support makes the argument easier to judge, and makes it obvious when a reason is missing or weak.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

opts.passage: My grandmother loves this park. Anyway, we should have the picnic here. It has covered tables in case it rains, and it's only a short walk from school.

nodes.text: The park has covered tables in case it rains.
The park is a short walk from school.
We should have the picnic at the park.

blocks.cap: The side remark about Grandma is left out of the standard form below the map.

blocks.title: Write it in standard form
blocks.q: "Every member of the art club must pay dues. Leo joined the art club in September, which was a rainy month. So Leo must pay dues."
steps: Conclusion: Leo must pay dues.
Reasons: every member must pay dues; Leo is a member.
The rainy month gives no reason, so leave it out.
Write: P1. Every member of the art club must pay dues. P2. Leo is a member of the art club. So: Leo must pay dues.
blocks.a: P1, P2, then "So: Leo must pay dues."

blocks.title: Keep the meaning
blocks.q: A premise says "Most of the apples are ripe." Is "All of the apples are ripe" a fair rewording?
steps: "Most" leaves room for some unripe apples; "all" does not.
Changing "most" to "all" makes the premise stronger than the speaker said.
blocks.a: No. Reword for clarity, never for strength.

blocks.html: Copying every sentence, including background and asides, or changing a premise's meaning while rewording it. Check each line of your standard form: is it a reason for the conclusion, and would the speaker agree it says what they said?

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (extended arguments)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Informal Logic"

blocks.html: In standard form every premise sits on its own line. But premises can work together in two different ways, and an argument map shows which.
Linked premises support the conclusion only together: take one away and the other gives no support. Convergent premises are separate reasons: each supports the conclusion by itself.

The difference matters when a premise turns out false. If premises are linked, one false premise breaks the whole support. If they are convergent, the other reasons still stand, and the case is only weaker.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: Every member of the art club signed up for the trip.
Noah is a member of the art club.
Noah signed up for the trip.
Noah's name is on the trip list.

blocks.cap: Premises 1 and 2 are linked (one box with +). Premise 4 is a separate, convergent reason.

blocks.title: The cover test
blocks.q: "We should take the bus to the museum. The bus is cheaper than a taxi. The bus stops right at the door."
steps: Cover the first reason. Does "the bus stops at the door" still give a reason to take the bus? Yes.
Cover the second. Does "the bus is cheaper" still give a reason? Yes.
Each works alone, so the premises are convergent.

blocks.title: Only together
blocks.q: "The hall holds 500 people. 500 tickets have been sold. So the concert is sold out."
steps: Cover the first premise: knowing 500 tickets were sold says nothing about sold out unless we know the size of the hall.
Cover the second: knowing the hall size alone says nothing about sales.
They support the conclusion only together.

blocks.html: Treating every pair of premises as linked. Use the cover test: remove one premise and ask whether the other still gives some support by itself. If it does, they are convergent.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Informal Logic"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (extended arguments)

blocks.html: Many arguments are built in steps. A claim supported by some premises can then be used as a premise for something further, like links in a chain.
A claim that is supported and then used to support another claim is an intermediate conclusion. The main conclusion is the claim that everything else finally supports.
Long arguments are easier to judge one step at a time. If an early step fails, everything built on it fails too, so it helps to see which claims hold up which.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: All the library's mystery books are on the second floor.
This book is a mystery from the library.
This book belongs on the second floor.
The cart is going to the second floor.
This book should go on the cart.

blocks.cap: Press Next to walk the chain from the main conclusion back to its first premises.

blocks.title: Two conclusions
blocks.q: "The cat hasn't eaten since yesterday, and it is hiding all day. So the cat is probably sick. Sick pets should see a vet soon. So we should take the cat to the vet."
steps: The first two sentences support "the cat is probably sick".
That claim then joins "sick pets should see a vet soon" to support the last sentence.
Nothing is offered as supported by "we should take the cat to the vet", so it is the main conclusion.
blocks.a: Intermediate: "The cat is probably sick." Main: "We should take the cat to the vet."

blocks.title: The last sentence is not always the main one
blocks.q: "We should move Saturday's game, because the field will likely flood. After all, heavy rain is forecast, and the field floods in heavy rain."
steps: "The field will likely flood" is supported by the forecast and the drainage fact.
It in turn supports "we should move Saturday's game", which comes first.
blocks.a: Main conclusion: "We should move Saturday's game."

blocks.html: Picking the intermediate conclusion as the main one because it has "so" in front of it. Both conclusions may have indicator words. Ask which claim is never used to support anything else: that is the main conclusion.

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (extended arguments)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Informal Logic"

blocks.html: People rarely say every step out loud. In a chain of reasoning or a short argument, a premise is often left for the listener to fill in.
An unstated premise is a claim the argument needs but does not say. Supply the most reasonable one: it should connect the stated premise to the conclusion, and the speaker should accept it.

Without the missing link, the stated premise does not reach the conclusion. "Rex is a dog, so Rex is a mammal" works only because we all know that dogs are mammals. Writing it down lets us check it, which is the whole point.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: The class garden gets six hours of sun.
Tomatoes grow well with six hours of sun.
We should plant tomatoes in the class garden.

blocks.cap: The dashed box is the unstated premise that links the sunshine to the tomatoes.

blocks.title: Fill the gap
blocks.q: "Mia is a member of the band, so Mia must go to Friday practice."
steps: Stated premise: Mia is a band member. Conclusion: Mia must go to Friday practice.
What links them? A claim about band members and Friday practice.
Most reasonable: "Every band member must go to Friday practice."
blocks.a: Unstated premise: "Every band member must go to Friday practice."

blocks.title: Not too strong
blocks.q: "The milk smells sour, so we shouldn't drink it." Which missing premise is best: "Sour-smelling milk is not safe to drink" or "We should never drink milk of any kind"?
steps: Both would make the conclusion follow.
The second is far stronger than the speaker needs, and the speaker clearly does not believe it.
Charity and accuracy both pick the first.
blocks.a: "Sour-smelling milk is not safe to drink."

blocks.html: Supplying a premise that just repeats the conclusion ("We shouldn't drink the milk"), or one much stronger than the speaker would accept. Check: does it link the stated premise to the conclusion, and would the speaker say "Yes, that's what I meant"?

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (extended arguments and missing premises)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Informal Logic"

blocks.html: Once you can find an argument's premises and conclusion, the next question is how strongly the premises are supposed to support it. Arguments make one of two kinds of promise.
A deductive argument claims that its conclusion must be true if its premises are true. An inductive argument claims only that its conclusion is probably true if its premises are.

The two kinds are judged by different standards. A deductive argument promises certainty, so a single possible exception breaks it. An inductive argument promises only likelihood, so we ask how likely, and new evidence can always raise or lower that.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: Every square has four sides, and this tile is a square, so it has four sides.
The last forty trains left on time, so tomorrow's train probably will too.
Ana is taller than Ben, and Ben is taller than Cam, so Ana must be taller than Cam.
cards.why: Specific to specific, yet the conclusion must follow.

cards.text: Most cats dislike baths, so Pepper will likely fuss at bath time.
Each of the three books on this shelf is a mystery, and there are only three, so every book on the shelf is a mystery.
cards.why: Specific to general, yet certain: every case was checked.

blocks.cap: Sort by the strength each argument claims, not by general or specific.

blocks.title: Listen for the promise
blocks.q: "Nine of the ten students we asked enjoy chess, so most students at our school probably enjoy chess."
steps: The word "probably" shows the promise: likelihood, not certainty.
It also reasons from a sample to a group, a typical inductive move.

blocks.title: Certain, from specific cases
blocks.q: "Ana is taller than Ben, and Ben is taller than Cam. So Ana is taller than Cam."
steps: If both premises are true, there is no way for the conclusion to be false.
It goes from specific facts to another specific fact, yet it is deductive.

blocks.html: Using the old rule "deduction goes from general to specific, induction from specific to general." Both examples above break it. Ask instead: does the argument claim its conclusion must follow, or only that it probably does? Words like must, necessarily, probably, likely are clues.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.4 Types of Inferences
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Deductive and Inductive Arguments"

blocks.html: A deductive argument promises that its conclusion must follow. When it keeps that promise, logicians call it valid.

An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false. Validity is about the link between premises and conclusion, not about whether they are actually true.

Validity comes from the form of an argument. "All B are C; all A are B; so all A are C" is valid whatever A, B and C are: if every A is inside B and every B is inside C, every A is inside C. Put in any words and the link holds.

blocks.title: Valid, with a false premise
blocks.q: "All penguins can fly. Pip is a penguin. So Pip can fly."
steps: The first premise is false: penguins cannot fly.
But imagine both premises were true. Then Pip would have to fly.
There is no way for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.
blocks.a: Valid (but, as we will see, not sound).

blocks.title: Invalid, though every statement is true
blocks.q: "All squares are rectangles. All squares are shapes. So all rectangles are shapes."
steps: Every statement here is true.
The form is: all A are B; all A are C; so all B are C.
Put other words in the same form: "All dogs are mammals. All dogs are pets. So all mammals are pets." The premises are true and the conclusion is false (wild bears are not pets).
So the form can fail, and the argument is invalid.
blocks.a: Invalid, even though everything in it is true.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: All whales are fish. Moby is a whale. So Moby is a fish.
cards.why: False premise, but if it were true the conclusion would follow.

cards.text: All robins are birds. Some birds are penguins. So some robins are penguins.
All squares are rectangles. All rectangles have four sides. So all squares have four sides.
All dogs are mammals. All cats are mammals. So all cats are dogs.
cards.why: Two things in the same group need not be the same thing.

blocks.cap: Imagine every premise is true. Could the conclusion still be false?

blocks.html: Calling an argument invalid because a premise is false, or valid because you agree with the conclusion. Validity ignores the facts. Test: pretend the premises are true. If the conclusion could still be false, the argument is invalid.

sources.name: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Validity and Soundness"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (validity, truth, soundness)

blocks.html: A valid form can never take true premises to a false conclusion. That gives us a test: to prove a form invalid, find one argument of that form that does exactly that.
The counterexample method: build an argument with the same form, whose premises are plainly true and whose conclusion is plainly false. One such argument proves the form invalid.

A valid form guarantees "true premises, true conclusion" for every argument of that form. So a single argument of the form with true premises and a false conclusion shows the guarantee fails, and the form is invalid. Every argument that shares the form shares the flaw.

blocks.title: Breaking a form
blocks.q: Show that this form is invalid: "All C are B. All A are B. So all A are C."
steps: Choose words for A, B and C that make both premises plainly true: C = dogs, B = mammals, A = cats.
Premises: "All dogs are mammals" (true). "All cats are mammals" (true).
Conclusion: "All cats are dogs" (plainly false).
Same form, true premises, false conclusion.

blocks.title: A failed attempt
blocks.q: Does "All dogs are animals. All mammals are animals. So all dogs are mammals." show the same form is invalid?
steps: It has the same form (C = mammals, B = animals, A = dogs).
But its conclusion, "All dogs are mammals", is true.
True premises with a true conclusion prove nothing about the form.
blocks.a: No. The conclusion must be false.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: All dogs are mammals. (true)
All cats are mammals. (true)
All cats are dogs. (false)

blocks.cap: A counterexample: two true premises leading, by the same form, to a false conclusion.

blocks.html: Changing the form while building the counterexample (for example, turning "All A are B" into "Some A are B"), or using premises that are not clearly true. Then the counterexample proves nothing. Check three things, in order: same form? premises plainly true? conclusion plainly false?

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (argument forms: proving invalidity)
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Validity and Soundness"

blocks.html: A valid argument has a good link, but its premises may be false. For an argument to prove its conclusion, it needs both a good link and true starting points.
An argument is sound when it is valid and all its premises are true. A sound argument's conclusion must be true.

Validity says: if the premises are true, the conclusion is true. Soundness adds: and the premises are true. Put the two together and the conclusion cannot escape being true. That is why a sound argument settles a question.

head: Valid?
All premises true?
Verdict
blocks.cap: Two questions, in order.

blocks.title: Sound
blocks.q: "All squares are rectangles. All rectangles have four sides. So all squares have four sides."
steps: Valid: if both premises are true, the conclusion must be.
Both premises are true.

blocks.title: Valid but not sound
blocks.q: "All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly."
steps: Valid: the form "All B are C; A is B; so A is C" never fails.
But "All birds can fly" is false (penguins and ostriches can't).

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: All whales are mammals. Moby is a whale. So Moby is a mammal.
All fish are mammals. Goldie is a fish. So Goldie is a mammal.
All dogs are mammals. Rex is a mammal. So Rex is a dog.
cards.why: Invalid: Rex could be a cat. A true conclusion would not save it.

cards.text: All squares are rectangles. All rectangles are polygons. So all squares are polygons.

blocks.cap: First ask if it is valid; only then check the premises.

blocks.html: Thinking a true conclusion makes an argument sound. "All dogs are mammals. Rex the dog is a mammal. So Rex is a dog" has a true conclusion, but its form is invalid, so it is not sound. Check validity first, then the premises; the conclusion's truth is not a test.

sources.name: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Validity and Soundness"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (validity, truth, soundness)

blocks.html: Validity and truth are separate. Soundness needs both. This lesson maps every way they can mix, so you are never surprised by a valid argument with a false conclusion.
A valid argument can have any mix of true and false premises and conclusion except one: all true premises with a false conclusion. An invalid argument can have any mix at all.

Validity is defined as "it is impossible for all the premises to be true and the conclusion false." It rules out exactly that one case and says nothing about the others. So from "valid" alone you cannot tell whether anything in it is true.

head: Premises
Conclusion
Valid example possible?
Invalid example possible?
blocks.cap: Only one box is empty.

blocks.title: Valid, false premises, true conclusion
blocks.q: Is "All fish are mammals. All whales are fish. So all whales are mammals." valid?
steps: Both premises are false.
The conclusion happens to be true.
The form "All B are C; all A are B; so all A are C" is valid.
blocks.a: Valid, and not sound, with a true conclusion.

blocks.title: Invalid, everything true
blocks.q: Is "All robins are birds. Some birds can fly. So all robins can fly." valid?
steps: All three statements are true.
Same form, other words: "All penguins are birds. Some birds can fly. So all penguins can fly." True premises, false conclusion.
So the form can fail.
blocks.a: Invalid, even though every statement in it is true.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: True premises, true conclusion
True premises, false conclusion
cards.why: This is the one mix validity rules out.

cards.text: A false premise, true conclusion
A false premise, false conclusion

blocks.cap: Sort each mix of truth values.

blocks.html: Believing a valid argument cannot have false premises or a false conclusion. It can have both. What it cannot have is all true premises and a false conclusion. If you know an argument has true premises and a false conclusion, you know for sure it is invalid.

sources.name: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Validity and Soundness"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (validity, truth, soundness)

blocks.html: An inductive argument does not promise certainty, so we do not call it valid or invalid. We ask how well it supports its conclusion.
An inductive argument is strong when its premises, if true, make the conclusion likely, and weak when they do not. A strong argument whose premises are actually true is cogent.

Inductive reasoning goes beyond its evidence: the next train has not left yet, however punctual the last forty were. So support comes in degrees, and new facts can always change it. A fact that gives a reason the pattern might break weakens the argument; a fact that rules out such reasons strengthens it.

head: Deductive
Inductive
blocks.cap: Matching words for the two kinds.

blocks.title: Strong or weak?
blocks.q: "Ben flipped a coin twice and got heads both times, so the coin will probably always land heads."
steps: Two flips are far too few to show a pattern; a fair coin does this one time in four.
If the premises are true, the conclusion is still not likely.

blocks.title: New facts
blocks.q: "Every time we have eaten at the Elm Diner, the food was good. So it will probably be good tonight." How does each fact change it? (a) The diner got a new cook last week. (b) The diner has blue booths.
steps: (a) gives a reason the pattern might break: the cook is the source of the good food. It weakens the argument.
(b) has nothing to do with the food. It makes no difference.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: It has snowed in Pine Hollow every January for fifty years, so it will probably snow there next January.
One student in the chess club likes chili, so most students probably like chili.
Ninety-eight of the hundred trees in the orchard bloomed in April, so the tree by the gate probably did too.

blocks.cap: If the premises are true, is the conclusion likely?

blocks.html: Calling a strong inductive argument "valid", or thinking a strong argument cannot be weakened. "Valid" is for deduction. And any inductive argument can be strengthened or weakened by more facts; that is part of what makes it inductive.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.4 Types of Inferences
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 1 (strength and cogency)

blocks.html: One common kind of inductive argument reasons from a sample to a whole group: "Most students I surveyed want a longer lunch, so most students at school do." How strong it is depends on the sample.
A generalization is only as good as its sample. A good sample is large enough and representative: chosen fairly, so it is like the whole group in the ways that matter to the question.

A sample stands in for a group we cannot check one by one. If it is tiny, chance can make it look very different from the group. If it is chosen in a slanted way, it will differ from the group in a steady direction, and making it bigger only repeats the slant.

blocks.title: Big but biased
blocks.q: To learn the favorite sport of students at a middle school, Jamal surveyed 300 people at a basketball game. Is this a good sample?
steps: 300 is a decent size.
But people at a basketball game are more likely than other students to love basketball.
The sample is not like the whole school on this question.
blocks.a: No: it is biased, however large.

blocks.title: Small but random
blocks.q: Rosa asked 4 friends whether students want more clubs. Is this a good sample of the school?
steps: Four people is far too few: a different four could give different answers.
Friends also tend to share interests.
blocks.a: No: too small (and probably not typical).

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: 200 students chosen at random from every grade
3 people at the lunch table
400 visitors to a chess website, asked about favorite games
cards.why: Large, but chess fans are not typical on this question.

cards.text: 150 people outside the pet store, asked how many people own a dog

blocks.cap: Two questions for every sample: big enough? chosen fairly?

blocks.html: Trusting a huge sample that was chosen in a biased way, like asking only chess club members which game students like best. Size does not cure bias. Ask how the people were chosen before asking how many there were.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.4 Types of Inferences
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 3 (hasty generalization) and the treatment of statistical reasoning

blocks.html: Another kind of inductive argument compares two things: they are alike in some ways, so they are probably alike in another. This is an argument from analogy.
An analogy is strong when the two things share features that are relevant to the conclusion, and differ only in ways that are not.

An analogy works because the shared features are a reason for the shared conclusion. A new bridge with the same design, steel and builders as an old, sturdy one will likely be sturdy, because design, steel and builders are what make a bridge strong. Its color is irrelevant, so a shared color adds nothing.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: The new bridge has the same design and steel as the old one.
The old bridge has held heavy trucks for forty years.
The new bridge will hold heavy trucks.
The new bridge is twice as long, with no extra supports.

blocks.cap: A relevant difference (length with no extra supports) weakens the analogy.

blocks.title: Which fact weakens it most?
blocks.q: "Ava's tomato plants and Ben's grow in the same soil and get the same sun. Ava's did well with weekly watering, so Ben's will too." (a) Ben's garden has a red gate. (b) Ben's plants are in small pots that dry out fast.
steps: Ask what the conclusion needs: plants that use water the same way.
(a) is a difference, but a gate has nothing to do with water.
(b) is a difference that matters for watering.

blocks.title: Count what matters
blocks.q: A dog and a cat are both furry pets with four legs. Dogs love fetching sticks. Does that make it likely the cat will?
steps: Fur and four legs have nothing to do with liking to fetch.
Many shared features, none relevant.

blocks.html: Counting similarities instead of weighing them. Ten irrelevant likenesses add nothing; one relevant difference can sink the argument. Ask: what does the conclusion depend on, and do the two cases share that?

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Analogy and Analogical Reasoning"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, the chapter on analogy and legal and moral reasoning

blocks.html: Many inductive arguments are about causes: this made that happen. They often start from a correlation, two things that tend to happen together.
Two things happening together does not show that one causes the other. Before concluding "A causes B", check for a common cause, a reversed direction, and coincidence.

A correlation fits several stories. Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together because sunny weather causes both. Towns with more firefighters have more fires because fires lead towns to hire firefighters, not the reverse. And with enough pairs of things, some will line up by chance. A cause claim needs evidence that rules these out, such as a fair test that changes one thing and holds the rest the same.

head: Pattern
Other explanation
Kind
rows: Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together
Towns with more firefighters have more fires
More fires lead to hiring more firefighters
The team won the day Kai wore green socks
blocks.cap: Three other stories to check.

blocks.title: Check the arrow
blocks.q: "People who visit the doctor more often are sick more often. So doctor visits make people sick."
steps: Is there a third thing causing both? Not an obvious one.
Could the arrow point the other way? Yes: being sick is what sends people to the doctor.

blocks.title: A fair test
blocks.q: Half of the bean plants, chosen at random, get fertilizer; the rest do not; everything else is kept the same. The fertilized ones grow taller. Is "the fertilizer helped" well supported?
steps: Random choice and equal care rule out a common cause.
We changed the fertilizer first, so the direction is clear.
A large, steady difference is unlikely to be chance.
blocks.a: Yes: this is good causal reasoning.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: Students who carry umbrellas are late more often.
cards.why: Rainy days cause both.

cards.text: Kids who sleep with a night light are more often afraid of the dark.
cards.why: Fear leads kids to ask for a light.

cards.text: A sneeze came just as the lights went out.

blocks.cap: Match each pattern to its likeliest other explanation.

blocks.html: Reading correlation as causation. Before you accept "A causes B", ask: could something cause both? Could B cause A? Could it be chance?

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, the chapter on causality and Mill's methods
OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.4 Types of Inferences

blocks.html: A statement is true or false, but only once we know what it says. Unclear words get in the way. Two kinds of unclearness are easy to confuse.
A word is ambiguous when it has two (or more) distinct meanings that both fit in context. A word is vague when it has one meaning but no sharp boundary.

The two need different fixes. Ambiguity is fixed by saying which meaning you intend ("a bat, the animal"). Vagueness is fixed by drawing a line ("tall, meaning over 180 cm"), which only matters when a decision depends on the edge.

head: Sentence
Word
Kind
rows: "I found a bat under the porch."
Ambiguous: an animal or a baseball bat
Vague: no exact height where tall begins
Ambiguous: a money bank or a riverbank
blocks.cap: Two meanings versus a blurry edge.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: "Ben said the soup was too hot." Is "hot" ambiguous or vague?
steps: Can "hot" mean two different things here? Yes: high in temperature, or spicy.
Both fit the sentence, so we cannot tell which Ben meant.
blocks.a: Ambiguous. (Within one meaning, "hot" is also vague, but the bigger problem here is the two meanings.)

blocks.title: One meaning, fuzzy edge
blocks.q: "The museum is close to the school."
steps: Does "close" have two separate meanings here? No: it means near.
But how near is close? A block? A mile? There is no exact cut-off.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: Kai saw a crane by the lake.
cards.why: A bird or a lifting machine.

cards.text: Wear something warm tomorrow.
The pitcher is on the table.
cards.why: A jug or a baseball player.

cards.text: The movie was long.

blocks.cap: Two meanings, or one meaning with a fuzzy edge?

blocks.html: Using "ambiguous" and "vague" as if they meant the same thing. Test: can you name two different meanings? Then it is ambiguous. Is there one meaning but no exact cut-off? Then it is vague.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Ambiguity"
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Vagueness"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 2 (language: meaning and definition)

blocks.html: One way to clear up ambiguity and vagueness is to define your words. But definitions do different jobs, and each job is judged differently.

A lexical definition reports how a word is already used. A stipulative definition gives a new word, or a new meaning, for a purpose. A precising definition sharpens a vague word. A persuasive definition slants a word to sway feelings.

A lexical definition is a report, so it can be accurate or mistaken. A stipulative one is a choice ("let's call this a frogurt bar"), so it can be clear or unclear but not false. A precising one must fit the old meaning while drawing a line. A persuasive one hides an argument inside a definition.

head: Kind
Example
Can it be false?
rows: "Triangle" means a closed shape with three straight sides.
In our club, a "zoomer" is anyone who solves a puzzle in under a minute.
For this contest, "tall" means 150 cm or more.
"Homework" means a cruel waste of evenings.
blocks.cap: Four jobs a definition can do.

blocks.title: Name the kind
blocks.q: "For the race rules, 'late' means arriving more than five minutes after the start."
steps: "Late" already has a meaning, but a fuzzy one.
This definition draws a sharp line for one purpose.

blocks.title: Report or choice?
blocks.q: "Let's call the new apple-and-yogurt snack a 'frogurt bar.'" Can this be false?
steps: It names something new; no one used "frogurt bar" for it before.
It is a choice, not a report about usage.
blocks.a: Stipulative, so it cannot be false (only clear or unclear).

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: "Library" means a place where books are kept for people to read or borrow.
A "true fan" is someone who never misses a single game.
For the reading challenge, a "book" is anything at least 50 pages long.
We'll call the third-floor reading nook "the Owl's Nest."

blocks.cap: Report, choose, sharpen, or slant?

blocks.html: Judging a stipulative definition as true or false. A new name for a new thing cannot be wrong, though it can be confusing. Ask first what job the definition is doing.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Definitions"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 2 (definitions and their purposes)

blocks.html: Of the kinds of definitions, the classical way to write a lexical one goes back to Aristotle: place the thing in a bigger group, then say what sets it apart.
A definition by genus and difference names the genus (the larger kind the thing belongs to) and the difference (the feature that sets it apart from the other members of that kind).

The genus tells you roughly where to look; the difference picks out exactly the right members. "A triangle is a polygon (genus) with three sides (difference)": every triangle is a polygon with three sides, and nothing else is.

head: Term
Genus
Difference
blocks.cap: Each definition in two parts.

blocks.title: Find the parts
blocks.q: "A peninsula is a piece of land that is almost surrounded by water but joined to the mainland."
steps: The bigger kind it belongs to: a piece of land. That is the genus.
What sets it apart from other pieces of land: almost surrounded by water but joined to the mainland. That is the difference.
blocks.a: Genus: piece of land. Difference: almost surrounded by water but joined to the mainland.

blocks.title: Not a definition
blocks.q: Which defines "island" by genus and difference? (a) "An island is a place like Hawaii." (b) "An island is an isle." (c) "An island is a piece of land surrounded by water."
steps: (a) gives an example, which tells you one island but not what makes something an island.
(b) gives a synonym, which helps only if you already know the other word.
(c) names a genus and a difference.

blocks.name: lg-sort

opts.task: Split "A kitten is a cat that is young" and "A carnivore is an animal that eats mainly meat" into parts.

cards.text: cat
that is young
animal
that eats mainly meat

blocks.cap: The genus is the bigger kind; the difference sets this thing apart within it.

blocks.html: Giving an example or a synonym instead of a definition, or naming a difference that other members of the genus also have ("A dog is an animal with four legs": so is a cat). Check: does the difference apply to all and only the things being defined?

sources.name: Aristotle, Topics, Book I (definition by genus and differentia)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Definitions"

blocks.html: A definition by genus and difference can still go wrong. Logic books list a few rules that catch the common faults.

A good definition is not too broad (it lets in nothing that doesn't belong), not too narrow (it leaves out nothing that does), not circular, not negative when it can be positive, and not figurative or obscure.

A definition should pick out exactly the right things and help someone who does not know the word. Too broad or too narrow picks out the wrong things. A circular definition uses the word itself, so it helps no one. A negative or figurative one leaves you not knowing what the thing is.

head: Definition
Fault
rows: A dog is an animal with four legs.
Too broad: cats have four legs
A bird is an animal with feathers that can fly.
A teacher is a person who teaches.
A circle is a shape that is not a square.
Music is the language of the heart.
blocks.cap: One example of each fault.

blocks.title: Broad or narrow?
blocks.q: "A chair is a wooden seat with four legs."
steps: Look for chairs it leaves out: metal chairs, plastic chairs, three-legged chairs.
It shuts out real chairs, so it is too narrow.
Does it let in non-chairs? A wooden stool with four legs, so it is also a little broad. The main fault is narrowness.

blocks.title: Circular
blocks.q: "A friend is someone who is friendly with you."
steps: "Friendly" is built from "friend".
Anyone who does not know what a friend is will not know what friendly means either.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.text: A shoe is a thing you wear.
cards.why: Hats are worn too.

cards.text: A pet is a dog or a cat.
cards.why: Goldfish and rabbits are pets too.

cards.text: A sandwich is food.
A vehicle is a car.

blocks.cap: Broad lets in extras; narrow leaves members out.

blocks.html: Mixing up too broad and too narrow. Too broad lets in things that do not belong (look for an outsider it includes). Too narrow shuts out things that do belong (look for a member it leaves out).

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 2 (criteria for lexical definitions)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Definitions"

blocks.html: Words do more than define and describe. Many also carry a feeling: praise or blame, warmth or scorn.
Emotive words express feelings as well as facts. Loaded language uses those feelings to win agreement in place of reasons: the slant does the arguing.

"The greedy owners jacked up prices" and "the owners raised prices" report the same fact. The first adds blame without adding evidence. If you agree with it, ask yourself whether you were given a reason or just a feeling.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: The greedy shop owners jacked up the price of tacos.
Only a fool would keep shopping at that rip-off store.

opts.name: Loaded language
opts.note: Words like greedy, jacked up, fool and rip-off push a feeling. The only fact is that prices went up.
opts.fix: The shop raised the price of tacos. If the new price is higher than other shops charge, we might buy them elsewhere.

blocks.cap: The loaded words are marked. The fair version below keeps the facts and the reasoning.

blocks.title: Neutral version
blocks.q: Rewrite neutrally: "The lazy referee blew another call."
steps: "Lazy" and "blew" add blame without evidence.
The fact underneath: the referee made a call some fans disagreed with.
blocks.a: "The referee made a call that many fans disagreed with."

blocks.title: Praise can be loaded too
blocks.q: "Our heroic volunteers gave up their whole Saturday for the park."
steps: "Heroic" and "gave up" add warm praise.
The facts: volunteers spent Saturday working in the park.
Praise is fine in a thank-you speech; it would be loaded if offered as a reason to fund the park.
blocks.a: Neutral: "Our volunteers spent Saturday working in the park."

blocks.html: Some words are loaded only in context. "Cheap" can mean a good price or poor quality. Ask what feeling the speaker wants you to have, and whether the facts alone would give it to you.

Thinking neutral words are always better. Feelings are fine in a speech or a story. The trouble comes when slanted words stand in for evidence. Check: if you swap in neutral words, is any reason left?

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 2 (cognitive and emotive meaning)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Informal Logic"

blocks.html: Because many words are ambiguous or vague, people can disagree without really disagreeing about the world. They are using one word in two senses.
A factual disagreement is about how things are; more facts could settle it. A verbal disagreement comes from using a word in different senses; it ends once people agree on what the word means.

Arguing harder about facts cannot settle a verbal dispute, because the two sides already agree on the facts. Spotting it saves time: say what each side means by the word, and see whether anything is left to disagree about.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: A hot dog is a sandwich: it is meat in bread.
No way. A sandwich needs two separate slices of bread.

opts.name: A verbal disagreement
opts.note: They agree on what a hot dog is. They disagree about what "sandwich" means.

blocks.cap: The disagreement sits in one word.

blocks.title: Verbal or factual?
blocks.q: Tess: "Pluto is a planet; it goes around the sun." Omar: "Pluto isn't a planet; it hasn't cleared its path of other objects."
steps: Do they disagree about Pluto's facts? No: both accept that it orbits the sun and shares its path.
They use "planet" in two senses: anything big and round circling the sun, or the astronomers' 2006 definition.

blocks.title: A factual one
blocks.q: Leo: "The pool opens at nine." Grace: "No, it opens at ten."
steps: Both mean the same thing by "opens".
A posted schedule would settle it.

blocks.html: Some disputes are both: two people may mean different things by "rich" and also disagree about how much money someone has. Settle the meaning first; then see which facts are still in question.

Arguing about facts when the real disagreement is over a word, such as whether a hot dog "counts" as a sandwich. Ask: if we agreed on what the word means, would we still disagree? If not, the dispute was verbal.

sources.name: Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 2 (verbal and factual disputes)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Ambiguity"

blocks.html: You can now judge an argument's link: validity for deduction and strength for induction. Some bad links show up so often, and fool people so well, that they have names. These are the fallacies.

A fallacy is a common pattern of bad reasoning that can seem convincing. A formal fallacy is a flaw in the form, visible with the words replaced by letters. An informal fallacy is a flaw in the content: you must read what the premises say to see it.

Naming a pattern makes it easier to notice. "Everyone believes it, so it's true" sounds fine until you have a name for it (appeal to the people) and remember why popularity is not proof. The names are tools for asking a sharper question, not labels to win with.

head: Formal fallacy
Informal fallacy
rows: "If it rained, the grass is wet. The grass is wet. So it rained." The shape "If P then Q; Q; so P" is broken, whatever P and Q are.
"Everyone at school has this game, so it's the best game ever." You must read the premise to see that popularity is not quality.
blocks.cap: Form versus content.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: Everyone at the park is flying a kite today.
So kite flying must be the best way to spend a Saturday.
opts.name: Appeal to the people
opts.note: Many people doing something is not a reason it is the best choice for everyone.

blocks.cap: A first look at a named fallacy: the faulty step is marked and named.

blocks.title: A fallacy with a true conclusion
blocks.q: "Most people I know think the Pacific is the largest ocean, so it is." Is the conclusion false?
steps: The Pacific is in fact the largest ocean, so the conclusion is true.
But what most people think is not what makes it true; measurement is.
The argument is bad; its conclusion is true anyway.
blocks.a: No. The conclusion is true, but this argument does not show it.

blocks.html: Calling any false statement a fallacy, or deciding that a fallacious argument has a false conclusion. "Spiders have six legs" is false, but it contains no reasoning, so it is not a fallacy. And a bad argument can reach a true conclusion; it just fails to support it.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.5 Informal Fallacies
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 3 (fallacies in general)

blocks.html: The first group of fallacies are fallacies of relevance: their premises have nothing to do with the conclusion, though they may stir feelings that make them seem to. The most famous one turns from the argument to the arguer.
Attacking the person (ad hominem) rejects a claim by attacking the person who made it (their character, looks, age or motives) instead of answering the reasons they gave.

A reason is good or bad no matter who gives it. If a messy student points out that many classmates walk to the library, the walking is just as real. Attacking the speaker leaves the reasons untouched, so the conclusion is no closer to being shown false.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: Our class should recycle the paper we throw away. Most of it is clean and could be used again.
You just want to look good for the teacher.
So forget about recycling.

opts.name: Attacking the person (ad hominem)
opts.note: Leo never answers Maya's reason (the paper could be reused). He guesses at her motives instead.
opts.fix: Leo: Is most of it really clean? Last week a lot of it had food on it.

blocks.cap: The faulty step, and a fair reply that answers the reason.

blocks.title: Spot the attack
blocks.q: "Dr. Lee has shown that the new bridge can hold twice the weight it needs to. But Dr. Lee is grumpy and never waves to the neighbors. So the bridge is probably unsafe."
steps: Dr. Lee's reason: the load tests.
The reply attacks Dr. Lee's friendliness, which has nothing to do with the tests.
blocks.a: Ad hominem: the second sentence attacks the person, not the tests.

blocks.html: Questioning a witness can be fair. If someone claims to have seen the missing bike but was across town at the time, doubting their report is good reasoning: the question is whether to trust what they say, not whether their argument is sound.

Calling every criticism of a person ad hominem. It is a fallacy only when the attack is used in place of answering the reasons. When the question is whether to trust someone's report, their honesty and position are relevant.

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.5 Informal Fallacies
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 3 (fallacies of relevance)

blocks.html: A close cousin of attacking the person points out that the person giving advice does not follow it.
You too (tu quoque) dismisses an argument or advice because the person who gave it does not act on it themselves.

Whether advice is good depends on the reasons for it, not on the adviser's habits. A helmet protects your head in a fall whether or not the person telling you to wear one wore theirs last week. Hypocrisy may be a fair complaint about the person; it is not evidence about the advice.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: You should wear a helmet when you ride. It protects your head in a fall.
You rode without a helmet last week, so why should I wear one?

opts.name: You too (tu quoque)
opts.note: Ava's slip does not change what a helmet does in a fall. Ben answers the person, not the reason.

blocks.cap: Pointing at the adviser instead of the advice.

blocks.title: Inconsistent, but right
blocks.q: The dentist tells Sam to floss every night. Sam says: "I saw the dentist eat a whole bag of candy, so I don't need to floss."
steps: The dentist's reason: flossing prevents cavities.
The candy is about the dentist's habits, not about flossing.
The reason still stands.

blocks.html: It is fair to bring up someone's past when the question is about them, for example, whether to trust their plan with the club's money after they spent it on snacks last year.

Treating hypocrisy as a refutation. A smoker who says smoking harms health may be inconsistent, but the evidence about smoking is the same either way. Ask: does the reply answer the reason, or only the person?

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.5 Informal Fallacies
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 3 (fallacies of relevance)

blocks.html: Some fallacies of relevance do talk about the other side's view, but not the real one.
A straw man replaces the other side's actual position with a weaker or more extreme version, knocks that version down, and claims victory.

Refuting a view only matters if it is the view someone holds. Knocking down "ban pizza forever" says nothing about "add more vegetables." The real proposal is still standing, untouched, after the attack.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: I think we should add more vegetables to the school lunch menu.
So you want to ban pizza forever and make everyone eat only salad?
That's ridiculous, so the menu should stay the same.

opts.name: Straw man
opts.note: Maya asked for more vegetables. Leo attacks a far more extreme plan she never offered.
opts.fix: Leo: If we add vegetables, which dish would we drop? The menu only has room for so many.

blocks.cap: The distorted copy, and a fair reply to the real view.

blocks.title: Compare the two versions
blocks.q: Ana: "Maybe we could shorten recess by five minutes on test days." Kai: "Ana wants to cancel recess for the whole year! Nobody should agree to that."
steps: Ana's view: five minutes, test days only.
Kai's version: no recess all year.
Kai attacks the second, which is much easier to reject.

blocks.title: A fair reply
blocks.q: Ana: "Maybe we could shorten recess by five minutes on test days." Kai: "Five minutes is small, but recess helps some students focus, so the trade might not raise scores."
steps: Kai states Ana's view accurately: five minutes, test days.
Then he gives a reason against that very view.
blocks.a: Not a straw man: Kai disagrees fairly.

blocks.html: Confusing straw man with red herring (next lesson). A straw man still talks about the opponent's view, only a distorted copy of it. Test: put the original claim and the attacked claim side by side. Are they the same?

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.5 Informal Fallacies
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 3 (fallacies of relevance)

blocks.html: A straw man twists the other side's view. A red herring leaves it behind altogether.
A red herring changes the subject to a different issue, then treats the original question as if it had been settled.

The new topic may be true and even interesting, but it is not about the question. Talking about how splintery the old playground was does not show that the new slide is cool enough to use. The first question is still open.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: The new slide is too hot to use in the afternoon sun.
The old playground had splinters everywhere, and the new one cost a lot of money.
So the slide is fine.

opts.name: Red herring
opts.note: Splinters and cost are different issues. Neither answers whether the slide is too hot.

blocks.cap: Tap the sentence where the subject changes, then press Check.

blocks.title: A dropped question
blocks.q: Parent: "Did you feed the dog this morning?" Child: "Did you know dogs are some of the smartest pets? So the dog is fine."
steps: The question: was the dog fed?
The reply: facts about dogs in general.
The reply is treated as if it settled the question.

blocks.title: Same topic, not a red herring
blocks.q: Ava: "The bake sale lost money because we bought too many supplies." Ben: "We also sold fewer cookies because it rained, so supplies were only part of it."
steps: Ben's point is about the same question: why the sale lost money.
He adds a cause; he does not change the subject.

blocks.html: Calling any change of topic a red herring. Raising a new topic openly is fine. It is a fallacy when the new topic is used as though it answered the first. Ask: after the reply, has the original question been answered?

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.5 Informal Fallacies
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies"
Patrick Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, chapter 3 (fallacies of relevance)

blocks.html: Some fallacies of relevance replace reasons with pressure. The bluntest kind is a threat.
An appeal to force tries to win agreement by a threat of harm (to someone's body, place, friendships or chances) instead of by reasons.

A threat can make people say they agree, but it gives no evidence that the claim is true. Whether a poster has a spelling mistake does not change because someone will kick you out of the group for mentioning it.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: I think the club should vote on the trip instead of just going to the zoo.
Keep saying that and I'll make sure you don't get picked for anything this year.
So we're going to the zoo.

opts.name: Appeal to force
opts.note: Nora gives no reason the zoo is a good choice. She only threatens Sam.

blocks.cap: A threat in place of a reason.

blocks.title: Threat or warning?
blocks.q: Coach: "If you skip practice this week, you'll be less ready for Saturday's game. So come to practice."
steps: Being less ready is a natural result of missing practice, not a punishment the coach will hand out.
It is relevant to the conclusion: it is a reason to come.
blocks.a: Not a fallacy: a fair warning.

head: Warning (fair)
Threat (fallacy)
rows: "If you skip practice, you'll play worse."
"Agree that my play is best, or you're on the bench."
"If we don't water the trees, they'll dry out."
"Say the food is great, or you're not invited."
blocks.cap: A natural result versus a penalty for disagreeing.

blocks.html: Calling every warning of a consequence an appeal to force. "If you skip practice, you'll play worse" gives a reason. "Agree with me or you're off the team" gives a threat. Ask: is the bad result a natural effect, or a punishment for disagreeing?

blocks.html: Like the appeal to force, this fallacy works on feelings, but it uses sympathy instead of fear.
An appeal to pity asks us to accept a claim because of sympathy for someone, when the sympathy has no bearing on whether the claim is true.

Feelings are real and often matter, but they cannot change facts. If an essay earned a C, a hard night does not turn it into A work. Pity is relevant to some questions (whether to give more time) and irrelevant to others (what grade the work deserves).

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: I should get an A on my essay.
I stayed up all night, my dog was sick, and I'll be so upset if I don't get an A.
opts.name: Appeal to pity
opts.note: Being tired and upset is sad, but it does not show the essay earned an A.
opts.fix: My dog was sick last night and I was at the vet. Could I have one more day to finish the essay?

blocks.cap: Sympathy used as evidence; the fair version asks for something sympathy can support.

blocks.title: Relevant or not?
blocks.q: "My drawing should win the contest. I've never won anything in my life, and it would mean so much to me."
steps: The question: which drawing is best?
Never having won makes us feel for the artist, but it says nothing about the drawing.

blocks.title: Pity that fits
blocks.q: "Mia's family lost their home in a flood. So our class could collect supplies to help them."
steps: The conclusion is about helping, not about what is true.
Sympathy is a fitting reason for kindness.

blocks.html: Thinking feelings are always irrelevant. Hardship can be a good reason for mercy, extra time or help. The fallacy is using pity to show that something is true, such as that a grade was earned or an answer is right.

blocks.html: Another fallacy of relevance leans on the crowd. It is sometimes called the bandwagon.
An appeal to the people argues that a claim is true, or a choice is good, because many people believe it or do it.

Large numbers of people have believed false things, and popular choices can be popular for reasons of fashion, price or habit. How many people believe a claim tells us about the people, not about the claim.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: Millions of people read their horoscope every morning.
So horoscopes must predict the future.
opts.name: Appeal to the people
opts.note: How many people read horoscopes says nothing about whether they work.

blocks.cap: The crowd as evidence.

blocks.title: When popularity is the point
blocks.q: "This cookbook is the best-selling cookbook in the state this year, so it is a very popular cookbook."
steps: Here the conclusion is about popularity itself.
Sales are exactly the right evidence for that.

blocks.title: When it is not
blocks.q: "Most of my friends skip breakfast, so skipping breakfast must be good for you."
steps: The conclusion is about health, not about what is common.
What many friends do is no evidence about what is good for the body.

blocks.html: Popularity is also relevant when the question is what people want: if nearly every student votes for tacos at the class party, that is a good reason to serve tacos.

Calling any mention of popularity a fallacy. Popularity is relevant to claims about popularity ("best-selling") and to choices meant to please many people. It is a fallacy when the conclusion is about truth or quality.

blocks.html: An appeal to the people leans on many voices. An appeal to authority leans on one voice that is supposed to know. Sometimes that is good reasoning; sometimes it is not.

Citing an expert in their own field, where experts agree, is reasonable. Citing someone outside their expertise, or one voice against a strong consensus, is the fallacy of appeal to unqualified authority.

Nobody can check everything, so we rely on people who know. That reliance is justified only when the person knows about this question. A soccer star knows soccer, not nutrition. One doctor against nearly all doctors gives weak evidence, because the field as a whole is a better guide than one member.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: A famous soccer star says this cereal makes you smarter.
So it must make you smarter.
opts.name: Appeal to unqualified authority
opts.note: Fame in sports is not expertise in nutrition or learning.

blocks.cap: An authority outside their field.

blocks.title: Fair
blocks.q: "The pediatrician who has treated children for twenty years says Ava needs to rest her sprained ankle for a week. So Ava should rest it."
steps: The question is medical, and the doctor is a medical expert.
Doctors broadly agree on resting sprains.

blocks.title: Unfair
blocks.q: "One doctor online says people should never drink water during exercise. Almost all other doctors say the opposite. So Kai stops drinking water at practice."
steps: The source is a doctor, so the field is right.
But it is one voice against nearly all experts.

blocks.html: Thinking every appeal to authority is a fallacy. We rely on experts all the time, and rightly. Ask two questions: is this person an expert on this very question, and do other experts in the field agree?

sources.name: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, 5.5 Informal Fallacies

blocks.html: The last fallacy of relevance builds a conclusion out of what we don't know.
An appeal to ignorance argues that a claim is true because it has not been proved false, or false because it has not been proved true.

Not having evidence is not the same as having evidence of the opposite. No one has proved there are no ghosts in the old theater, but no one has proved there are, either. Either conclusion would be built on nothing.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: Nobody can prove that my lucky socks don't help me score goals.
So they must help.

opts.name: Appeal to ignorance
opts.note: A lack of disproof is not evidence that the socks help.

blocks.cap: A conclusion drawn from no evidence.

blocks.title: Unfair
blocks.q: "You can't prove I ate the last cookie, so I didn't eat it."
steps: The premise reports a lack of proof.
The conclusion claims a fact.
Nothing connects the two.

blocks.title: A careful search
blocks.q: "We checked every room, closet and shelf in the house and found no sign of the cat. So the cat is probably not in the house."
steps: This is not a mere lack of proof: there was a search that would very likely have found the cat.
A failed careful search is evidence.

blocks.html: Courts treat a person as innocent unless the evidence shows guilt. That is a rule about who must prove what, not a claim that a lack of proof shows innocence is a fact.

Treating every "we found nothing" as this fallacy. A careful search that should have found something counts as evidence ("we checked every room; the cat is not inside"). The fallacy treats a mere lack of proof as proof.

blocks.html: The next group of fallacies are fallacies of presumption: they slip in an assumption that has not been earned. Writing an argument in standard form is the best way to catch the first one.
An argument begs the question when a premise assumes the very conclusion it is supposed to prove, often in different words. It is circular reasoning.

A premise is supposed to be a reason you can accept before you accept the conclusion. If the premise is the conclusion in disguise, you can only accept it if you already agree, so the argument gives a doubter nothing.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: Pizza is the best food.
After all, no other food is better than pizza.
opts.name: Begging the question
opts.note: "No other food is better" is just "pizza is the best" said another way. The premise assumes the conclusion.

blocks.cap: The conclusion hiding inside the premise.

blocks.title: Say it in your own words
blocks.q: "Reading is good for you, because reading has a positive effect on people who do it."
steps: Restate the premise plainly: reading is good for people.
That is the conclusion again.

blocks.title: A circle through trust
blocks.q: "Sam always tells the truth. We know this because Sam told us so, and Sam never lies."
steps: To trust Sam's statement, we must already believe Sam is truthful.
That is the conclusion.

blocks.html: Compare: "Our team will probably win, because we beat this team twice this season and their best player is out sick." These reasons are independent of the conclusion, and you can check them, so nothing is begged.

In everyday speech, "that begs the question" often means "that raises the question." In logic it means circular reasoning: the conclusion hides in a premise. Test: put the premise in your own words. If you get the conclusion back, the question is begged.

blocks.html: A cousin of begging the question hides the assumption in a question instead of a premise.
A complex question has a hidden assumption built in, so that any direct answer grants it.

"Have you stopped forgetting your homework?" looks like a yes-or-no question. But "yes" admits you used to forget it, and "no" admits you still do. The question is really two: did you ever forget it, and do you still? A fair reply splits them apart.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: How long have you been hiding the truth about the missing trophy?

opts.name: Complex question
opts.note: Any number of days or weeks you answer grants that you were hiding the truth.
opts.fix: Reporter: Do you know anything about the missing trophy?

blocks.cap: A question that assumes its answer, and a fair version.

blocks.title: Find the hidden claim
blocks.q: "Why are you always so rude to the new students?"
steps: The question assumes the person is always rude to new students.
Any answer that starts "Because…" grants it.
blocks.a: Complex question. A fair reply: "I don't think I am. What did you see?"

head: Complex question
What it assumes
rows: Did you spend the club money on candy again?
You spent it on candy before
Where did you hide my toy?
blocks.cap: Look for words like "again", "still", "stopped" and "why".

blocks.html: Answering the question instead of spotting the assumption. "Have you stopped forgetting your homework?" assumes you used to forget it. Before answering, ask: what would I be agreeing to with a yes, and with a no?

blocks.html: Another fallacy of presumption assumes there are fewer choices than there really are.
A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones when others exist, then pushes you toward one by rejecting the other.

An either-or argument is valid: if it is A or B, and not B, then it is A. So the whole weight rests on the either-or premise. If there is a third option, that premise is false, and the argument proves nothing.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: Either we go to the lake on Saturday, or we sit at home and do nothing all weekend.
Nobody wants to do nothing, so we're going to the lake.

opts.name: False dilemma
opts.note: There are many other things to do this weekend besides those two.

blocks.cap: Two options offered as the only two.

blocks.title: Find the missing option
blocks.q: Coach: "Either we practice four hours a day, or we'll lose every game."
steps: Are those the only two possibilities?
No: practicing a bit more, or practicing more wisely, are other choices.

blocks.title: A real either-or
blocks.q: "A whole number is either even or odd. 7 is not even, so it is odd."
steps: Is there a third option? No: every whole number is even or odd.
With the either-or true, the step to "7 is odd" is good reasoning.

blocks.html: When you meet an either-or, try to finish the sentence "Or we could…". If you can, the dilemma is false, and the argument needs a new premise that rules your option out.
Treating every either-or as a false dilemma. "The light is on or it is off" really covers the cases. The fallacy needs a missing option. Test: can you name a third choice?

blocks.html: Now come the fallacies of weak induction: arguments whose premises give some support, but far too little. The first is the bad generalization.
A hasty generalization draws a conclusion about a whole group from a sample that is too small or not typical of the group.
A few cases can differ from the whole group by chance, and an unusual sample differs in a steady way. Two rude people from a town tell you about two people, not about the town.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: Ava met two people from Riverton who were rude.
So people from Riverton are rude.
opts.name: Hasty generalization
opts.note: Two people are far too few to tell us about a whole town.

blocks.cap: A leap from a few cases to the whole group.

blocks.title: Too small
blocks.q: "The first ten pages of the book were slow, so the whole book is boring."
steps: Ten pages is a small and possibly untypical part of the book.
Openings are often slower than the rest.

blocks.title: A fair sample
blocks.q: "The cook tasted a spoonful from the well-stirred pot of soup and it was too salty. So the whole pot is too salty."
steps: A well-stirred pot is the same throughout.
So one spoonful is a typical sample.

blocks.html: Two quick questions catch most hasty generalizations: how many cases were there, and how were they picked? A big, fairly chosen sample can support a general claim; a handful of cases picked by chance encounter cannot.

Confusing hasty generalization with accident (later in this unit). Hasty generalization goes up from a few cases to a rule. Accident goes down: it applies a good rule to a case the rule was not made for.

blocks.html: You met reasoning about causes earlier. When that reasoning skips the checks, it becomes a fallacy.
False cause claims that one thing caused another only because it came first (often called post hoc, "after this") or only because the two happen together.

Many things come before any event, and many things move together by chance or because of a third cause. Timing is a clue to look further, not a proof. Good causal claims rule out the other explanations.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: The new soccer coach started in March.
In April, the team won four games in a row.
So the new coach must be the reason the team is winning.
opts.name: False cause
opts.note: Coming first is not the same as causing. Easier opponents or a returning player could explain the wins.

blocks.cap: Tap the sentence where the reasoning goes wrong, then press Check.

blocks.title: After, so because?
blocks.q: "Kai started drinking orange juice every morning, and a week later the cold went away. So orange juice cured the cold."
steps: Colds usually clear up in about a week on their own.
The timing fits, but it would fit without the juice too.

blocks.title: Together, so because?
blocks.q: "Ice cream sales and sunburns rise in the same months. So ice cream causes sunburn."
steps: Could something else cause both? Yes: hot, sunny weather.
People buy more ice cream and get more sunburns on sunny days, so neither needs to cause the other.

blocks.html: Accepting "it happened right after, so it caused it." Before agreeing, look for other causes (what else changed?), reversed direction, and plain chance.
