blocks.html: A false cause claims one weak causal link. A slippery slope claims a whole chain of them.
A slippery slope argues that one step will set off a chain of events ending in disaster, without good reason to think each link in the chain will happen.

A chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and the chances multiply: if each of four links is only somewhat likely, the whole chain is unlikely. Presenting the end as certain hides how weak the links are.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences.text: If we let students drink water in class, next they'll want snacks, then full meals.
Soon class will be one big cafeteria, so no water bottles in class.

opts.name: Slippery slope
opts.note: Nothing shows that allowing water leads to full meals. Each link is only asserted.

blocks.cap: A chain of unsupported links.

blocks.title: Test each link
blocks.q: "If you skip one homework assignment, you'll fall behind, then fail the class, then never get into college."
steps: Does one missed assignment usually mean falling behind? Not usually.
Does falling a bit behind mean failing? No.
The links are weak, and the end is presented as certain.

blocks.title: A supported chain
blocks.q: "If you leave the milk out all day, it will warm up. Bacteria grow faster in warm milk. So the milk will likely spoil."
steps: Does warm milk follow from leaving it out? Yes.
Do bacteria grow faster when it is warm, and does that spoil milk? Yes: each link is a well-known fact.

blocks.html: Calling every chain of consequences a slippery slope. Some chains are well supported. The fallacy is a chain of weak or unsupported links presented as though the end were certain. Check each link on its own.

blocks.html: An argument from analogy can be strong. When the likenesses do not matter for the conclusion, it becomes a fallacy.
A weak analogy rests on likenesses that are not relevant to the conclusion, or ignores differences that are.

An analogy works only when the shared features are a reason for the shared conclusion. Bikes and cars both have wheels, but wheels have nothing to do with fuel, so the likeness gives no reason to think a bike needs gasoline.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: A school is like a business.
A business fires workers who don't make money.
So a school should expel students who get low grades.
opts.name: Weak analogy
opts.note: Schools exist to teach students, not to make money from them. The likeness fails in the way that matters.

blocks.cap: A comparison that breaks where the conclusion needs it.

blocks.title: Relevant or not?
blocks.q: "My bike and a car both have wheels and take you places. Cars need gasoline, so my bike needs gasoline too."
steps: What does the conclusion need? A shared way of being powered.
Wheels and travel are not about power.

blocks.title: A strong one
blocks.q: "This puzzle box has the same maker, lock and lid pattern as the last one, which opened by sliding the lid left. So this one probably does too."
steps: What does the conclusion need? A shared way of opening.
Maker, lock and pattern are exactly what decide how a box opens.

blocks.html: Calling every comparison weak. Ask what the conclusion needs, then check whether the two cases share that feature. If they do, and no relevant difference is ignored, the analogy can be strong.

blocks.html: An inductive argument can be weakened by new facts. This fallacy hides the fact that would do it.
Suppressed evidence leaves out an important fact that would change the conclusion, so true premises lead to a misleading conclusion.

Inductive support depends on all the evidence we have. A trail can be "only two miles long" and still be a terrible walk for small children if it climbs a cliff. Each stated fact is true; the conclusion is unreliable because of what was left out.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: The used bike has new tires and a shiny new paint job.
So it is a great bike to buy.
(The seller knows the frame is cracked.)
opts.name: Suppressed evidence
opts.note: A cracked frame changes everything. Leaving it out makes true premises mislead.

blocks.cap: True premises, a missing fact, a misleading conclusion.

blocks.title: What was left out?
blocks.q: "This snack has no added sugar, so it is a healthy snack." (It is deep-fried and very salty.)
steps: The premise is true.
But frying and salt matter for health, and they were left out.

blocks.title: Nothing hidden
blocks.q: "The trail is two miles long, mostly flat, with benches every half mile. So it is a good walk for little kids."
steps: What would a parent want to know? Length, steepness and places to rest.
All of those are given, and nothing important seems hidden.

blocks.html: Checking only whether the stated premises are true. A set of true premises can still mislead when a key fact is left out. Ask: what else would I want to know before accepting this?

blocks.html: The last fallacy of this unit is the mirror image of hasty generalization. There the rule was bad; here the rule is good but misapplied.
Accident applies a general rule to a special case that the rule was never meant to cover.

Most rules are made for ordinary cases and have unstated exceptions. "No running in the halls" is about safety on normal days; running out during a fire alarm serves the same safety goal. Forcing the rule onto the special case defeats its purpose.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: Speeding is against the law.
The ambulance was speeding to the hospital.
So the ambulance driver should get a ticket.
opts.name: Accident
opts.note: Speed limits are not meant to stop ambulances on emergency calls.

blocks.cap: A good rule forced onto an exception.

blocks.title: A special case
blocks.q: "People should keep their promises. Ava promised to meet Ben at noon, but she stopped to help a child who fell off a bike. So Ava did something wrong."
steps: Keeping promises is a good rule.
It was never meant to forbid helping someone who is hurt.

blocks.title: An ordinary case
blocks.q: "Library books are due in three weeks. Leo's book is five weeks old and nothing special delayed it. So Leo owes the late fee."
steps: Is anything special about this case? No: nothing delayed the book.
This is the very kind of case the rule was written for.

blocks.html: Calling this hasty generalization. In accident, the rule is fine in general; the mistake is forcing it onto an exception. In hasty generalization, the rule itself was drawn from too few cases.

blocks.html: The fallacies of ambiguity slide between two meanings. The simplest one rides on a single ambiguous word.
Equivocation uses a word in one sense in one premise and in another sense elsewhere, so the argument only seems to connect.

An argument links its premises through shared words. If the word changes meaning, the link is broken, even though the spelling hides the break. With the meanings written out, the premises are about two different things.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: A feather is light.
What is light cannot be dark.
So a feather cannot be dark.
opts.name: Equivocation
opts.note: "Light" means not heavy in the first line and bright in the second.
opts.fix: Write the meanings out: "A feather is not heavy. What is bright cannot be dark." Now nothing connects.

blocks.cap: One spelling, two meanings, no real link.

blocks.title: Swap in the meanings
blocks.q: "Ben is a big fan of the town team. A fan is a machine that blows air. So Ben is a machine that blows air."
steps: Line 1: "fan" means a supporter.
Line 2: "fan" means a machine.
Replace each with its meaning: the premises no longer share a term.

blocks.title: Hidden in "nothing"
blocks.q: "Nothing is better than a long vacation. A cold sandwich is better than nothing. So a cold sandwich is better than a long vacation."
steps: First "nothing": no other thing (no thing beats a vacation).
Second "nothing": having nothing at all.
Two senses, so the chain breaks.

blocks.html: Missing the shift because the spelling stays the same. Replace the word with what it means in each line; if the two meanings differ, the gap shows at once.

blocks.html: Equivocation rides on one word. Amphiboly rides on the grammar of a whole sentence.
Amphiboly draws a conclusion from a sentence whose grammar allows two readings, using the reading its writer did not mean.

Loose grammar can attach a phrase to the wrong word. "We sell dresses for girls with lace" means dresses with lace, but the grammar lets "with lace" attach to "girls." An argument built on the unintended reading starts from a premise nobody asserted.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: The sign said: "Slow children at play."
So the children who play here must be slow runners.
opts.name: Amphiboly
opts.note: The sign tells drivers to slow down because children play there. Its grammar allows a silly second reading.

blocks.cap: A sentence that can be read two ways.

blocks.title: Two readings
blocks.q: "Ava saw the hiker with binoculars. So the hiker had binoculars."
steps: Reading 1: Ava used binoculars to see the hiker.
Reading 2: the hiker was carrying binoculars.
The conclusion picks reading 2 with no reason.

blocks.title: Word or grammar?
blocks.q: "The menu said: 'Free soup and salad with any taco.' So the salad is free, but the soup costs money."
steps: No single word changes meaning.
The question is whether "free" covers both items: a grammar question.

head: Equivocation
Amphiboly
blocks.cap: Where the double meaning lives.

blocks.html: Confusing amphiboly with equivocation. In equivocation one word has two meanings; in amphiboly the sentence structure does. Ask: could I fix it by defining a word, or only by rearranging the sentence?

blocks.html: The last two fallacies of this unit move a property between a whole and its parts. Both trade on an ambiguity between saying something of each part and saying it of the whole.
Composition reasons that because every part has a property, the whole must have it too.

Some properties add up and some do not. If every brick is red, the wall is red. But if every brick is light, the wall is not light: weight adds up. Great players can make a poor team, because playing well together is not the sum of playing well alone.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: Each brick in the wall is light enough to lift with one hand.
So the whole wall is light enough to lift with one hand.
opts.name: Composition
opts.note: Weight adds up. Many light bricks make a heavy wall.

blocks.cap: From the parts to the whole.

blocks.title: Does it add up?
blocks.q: "Every song on the album is short, so the album is short."
steps: Each part: a short song. The whole: the album.
Length adds up: many short songs can make a long album.

blocks.title: It carries over
blocks.q: "Every piece of the puzzle is made of wood, so the puzzle is made of wood."
steps: What something is made of carries over from its parts.
A whole made only of wooden pieces is wooden.

blocks.html: Assuming every property fails to carry over. Some do (color, material: if every brick is red, the wall is red). Ask whether this particular property is one that adds up or changes when parts come together.

blocks.html: Composition goes from the parts to the whole. Division goes the other way.
Division reasons that because the whole has a property, each part must have it too.

A whole can have properties that come from how its parts work together or add up. An orchestra can be famous while its players are not; a class can raise a lot of money from many small gifts. The property belongs to the whole, not to each part.

blocks.name: lg-fallacy

sentences: The class raised a lot of money for the animal shelter.
So each student raised a lot of money.
opts.name: Division
opts.note: A large total can come from many small gifts.

blocks.cap: From the whole to the parts.

blocks.title: Does it pass down?
blocks.q: "The cake is sweet, so the flour in it is sweet."
steps: The cake is sweet because of the sugar.
Sweetness of the whole does not pass to every ingredient.

blocks.title: It passes down
blocks.q: "The whole fence is painted white, so each board of the fence is painted white."
steps: If all of the fence is white, each board is white.
Color spread over the whole passes to each part.

head: Composition
Division
rows: Every player is great, so the team is great.
The team is great, so every player is great.
blocks.cap: Same mistake, opposite directions.

blocks.html: Mixing up composition and division. Composition goes from the parts up to the whole; division goes from the whole down to the parts. Find which one the premise is about and which one the conclusion is about.

blocks.html: The counterexample method shows a form is invalid. Here we use it on the most common formal fallacies, which start from an "if… then…" premise.
From "If P, then Q": you may infer Q from P (modus ponens), and not-P from not-Q (modus tollens). You may not infer P from Q (affirming the consequent) or not-Q from not-P (denying the antecedent).

"If it rained, the street is wet" says rain is one way to get a wet street. So rain guarantees a wet street, and a dry street rules out rain. But a wet street does not tell you it rained (a sprinkler could have done it), and no rain does not tell you the street is dry, for the same reason.

sentences: If it rained last night, the street is wet.
The street is wet.
So it rained last night.
opts.name: Affirming the consequent
opts.note: A sprinkler or a street cleaner could have wet the street.

blocks.cap: The faulty step: concluding the "if" part from the "then" part.

blocks.title: Name the form
blocks.q: "If the dog is hungry, it barks at the door. It is barking at the door. So it is hungry."
steps: The second premise says the "then" part happened (it is barking).
The conclusion is the "if" part (it is hungry).
It might bark because it wants to go out.

blocks.title: A valid one
blocks.q: "If Ben won the race, he got a medal. Ben did not get a medal. So Ben did not win."
steps: The second premise denies the "then" part.
If Ben had won, he would have a medal; he doesn't, so he didn't win.

blocks.html: Affirming the consequent feels natural: "If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet, so it rained." Before accepting, ask: what else could make the "then" part true? A counterexample with the same form: "If it is a dog, it is a mammal. It is a mammal. So it is a dog" (it could be a cat).

blocks.html: You have met over twenty fallacies, from red herring to division. Several come in look-alike pairs. Naming the right one is a test of whether you see what the reasoning does.

Name a fallacy by the job the faulty step does: distorting a view, changing the subject, leaping from a sample, misapplying a rule, assuming the conclusion, and so on. Find the faulty step first; then ask what it does.

Surface words mislead. "Everyone" appears in arguments that are fine; "expert" appears in fair appeals to authority. Two passages about a menu can commit different fallacies. Only the job of the faulty step tells you which name fits.

head: Look-alikes
How to tell them apart
rows: Twists the other view / drops it for another topic
Few cases up to a rule / a good rule down to an exception
Parts to whole / whole to parts
One word, two meanings / one sentence, two structures
One weak causal link / a chain of them
Begging the question / appeal to ignorance
Conclusion hidden in a premise / lack of proof taken as proof
blocks.cap: Six pairs worth knowing.

cards.text: Two people from Lakeside were rude, so people from Lakeside are rude.
Exercise is good for you, so Max should run even with a broken leg.
The first five pages were slow, so the whole book is boring.
Sharing is good, so share your test answers with the class.

blocks.cap: Up from a few cases, or a good rule pushed onto an exception?

blocks.title: Straw man or red herring?
blocks.q: Ava: "We should plant a few more trees on Main Street." Ben: "Our town has the best summer fair in the county, so Main Street is fine."
steps: Does Ben attack a twisted version of Ava's plan? No.
He changes the subject to the fair and treats the question as settled.

blocks.title: Composition or division?
blocks.q: "The orchestra is famous, so each player in it must be famous."
steps: The premise is about the whole (the orchestra).
The conclusion is about the parts (each player).
Whole to parts.

blocks.html: Matching on surface words like "everyone" or "expert" rather than on what the reasoning does. Find the faulty step first, then name it by its job.

blocks.html: Learning fallacy names has a risk: seeing fallacies everywhere. Many fallacies have a fair cousin that looks similar but reasons well, like the fair appeals to authority you have met.
A fallacy name fits only when its faulty step is really there. Trusting real experts, following a well-supported chain of causes, and naming a real either-or are good reasoning, not fallacies.

Each fallacy is defined by a specific failure: an irrelevant attack, a missing option, unsupported links, a biased sample. If the passage does not contain that failure, the name does not apply, however familiar the surface looks.

head: Looks like…
But is fair when…
rows: the question is whether to trust a witness's report
the source is an expert in this field and experts agree
each link in the chain is well supported
the two options really cover every case
a careful search would have found the thing
the conclusion is about kindness or help, not truth

cards.why: Buddy systems and more chaperones are other options.

cards.text: Weather scientists expect heavy rain, so we should move the picnic indoors.
A movie star says this car is the safest one, so it is.

blocks.cap: Is the faulty step really there?

blocks.title: Fair or fallacy?
blocks.q: "If we spend the trip money on snacks, we won't have enough for the bus. Without the bus, the class can't get to the museum. So we shouldn't spend it on snacks."
steps: It is a chain of consequences, like a slippery slope.
But each link is a plain fact about money and travel.

blocks.title: Fair or fallacy?
blocks.q: "Nobody has proved the new paint is safe for the class hamster, so the paint must be poisonous."
steps: A lack of proof that it is safe is offered as proof that it is poisonous.
Caution would be wise, but the conclusion claims too much.

blocks.html: Fallacy hunting: shouting a fallacy name at every argument you dislike. Each name fits only when its faulty step is really there. If you cannot point to the step, withdraw the name.

blocks.html: Before judging an argument you must state it, often filling in unstated premises. How you fill them in matters. A twisted version is a straw man.
The principle of charity: before judging an argument, state it in its strongest reasonable form, the way its author would accept.

If you reject a weak version of an argument, you have learned nothing about the real one, and the author can rightly say you missed the point. Judging the strongest reasonable version means that if you still find it weak, your judgment counts.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: The library closes at five.
Many students cannot get there before five.
If many students can't visit before five, later hours would let them use it.
The library should stay open later.

blocks.cap: A charitable unstated premise: just what the argument needs, and something the speaker would accept.

blocks.title: Restate fairly
blocks.q: Max says: "We should have less homework on weekends." Which restatement is charitable? (a) "Weekend homework should be lighter, so students have time to rest." (b) "Max thinks students should never do any work."
steps: (a) keeps Max's claim and gives it a sensible reason.
(b) turns it into an extreme view he never stated.

blocks.title: Fill the gap charitably
blocks.q: "The dog needs a bigger cage. It can barely turn around." Which premise fills the gap?
steps: Option: "An animal that can barely turn around in its cage needs more room." It links the premise to the conclusion and is easy to accept.
Option: "Every animal should live in the biggest cage ever built." It is much stronger than needed and makes the speaker look silly.

blocks.html: Reading charity as agreeing. Charity is about understanding the argument fairly. After that, you may still find it weak, and you should say so.

blocks.html: Now put the course together. A charitable reading tells you what the argument is. Validity and truth and the conditional forms tell you how to judge it.

Evaluate an argument in steps: (1) find the conclusion and premises; (2) ask whether the premises support the conclusion (valid, or strong); (3) ask whether the premises are true. A good argument passes both (2) and (3).

Questions (2) and (3) are separate, and each can fail on its own. An argument with true premises can still fail to support its conclusion, and a perfect link can start from a false premise. Asking them separately tells you exactly what is wrong, which is more useful than "I disagree."

items: Link: deductive? check validity. Inductive? check strength. Watch for named fallacies.
Truth: are the premises true, as far as you can tell?
Verdict: good (sound or cogent), or say which step fails.

opts.passage: All mammals breathe air. Whales are mammals. So whales breathe air.

nodes.text: All mammals breathe air.
Whales are mammals.
Whales breathe air.

blocks.cap: Step 1 done: the argument in a map and in standard form. Steps 2 and 3 are below.

blocks.title: A good argument
blocks.q: Evaluate: "All mammals breathe air. Whales are mammals. So whales breathe air."
steps: Conclusion: whales breathe air. Premises: all mammals breathe air; whales are mammals.
Link: "All B are C; A are B; so A are C" is valid.
Truth: both premises are true.

blocks.title: Which step fails?
blocks.q: Evaluate: "All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly."
steps: Link: same valid form as before.
Truth: "All birds can fly" is false.
blocks.a: It follows, but a premise is false: not sound.

blocks.html: Jumping to "I disagree with the conclusion" without asking the two separate questions: does it follow, and are the premises true? Disagreeing with a conclusion tells you to look closer; it does not tell you which step is wrong.

blocks.html: Once you can evaluate an argument, you can also make a case stronger by facing what can be said against it. An objection is a reason to doubt an argument; a reply answers it.
An objection attacks either a premise (saying it is false) or the link (granting the premises but denying that the conclusion follows). A strong case answers the best objection, not the weakest.

Knowing what an objection attacks tells you how much it can do. Knocking out one of several convergent premises weakens a case; knocking out one of two linked premises breaks it. And an objection to the link ("even if that's all true…") can defeat an argument with entirely true premises.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: The class garden gets six hours of sun.
Tomatoes grow well with six hours of sun.
We should plant tomatoes in the class garden.
Squirrels in the yard eat tomatoes.
A simple net keeps squirrels out.

blocks.cap: An objection to the conclusion, and a reply that answers it.

blocks.title: What does it attack?
blocks.q: Argument: "The picnic should be at the park. P1: It has covered tables. P2: It is a short walk." Objection: "Even if both are true, the park's fee is more than our budget."
steps: Does the objection say P1 or P2 is false? No: it says "even if both are true."
It says something else matters, so the conclusion does not follow.

blocks.title: Does the case survive?
blocks.q: Same argument. Objection: "The covered tables were taken down last month."
steps: This denies P1.
P1 and P2 are convergent: the short walk is still a separate reason.
The case is weaker but not gone.
blocks.a: No, the conclusion keeps some support from P2.

blocks.html: Answering a weak objection and calling the case closed, or thinking that knocking out one premise defeats a conclusion that has other, independent support. Check whether the premises are linked or convergent, and look for the strongest objection.
